WHITE CAP OUTRAGES CONTINUE.
Terrible Outrage on a Cattle Buyer in Ohio—Titusville, Pa., Has Them Too.

WINCHESTER, O., Dec. 21.—A terrible outrage occurred five miles south of here Wednesday night, in the very heart of the White Cap country. Three masked men robbed Z. H. Cutter, a Cincinnati cattle buyer, of $1,000, beat him shamefully, tied him to his horse Mazeppa fashion, and started the animal off on a dead run. Cutter was accidentally found at midnight, almost dead.

TITUSVILLE, Pa., Dec. 21.—It is now definitely settled that a White Cap organization infests this city. Within the past two weeks twenty letters have been sent to parties here, women as well as men, notifying them that if their conduct is not more proper in the future the lash will be applied. These letters were at first taken as a joke, but they have assumed a more serious character of late. The editors of The Herald and of The Sunday World have both received letters. A counter organization is going to be formed to offset the White Caps and to protect law abiding citizens.

CANTON, O., Dec. 21.—The White Caps have shown their hand here. W. J. Cole, who forced his wife to leave home a few days ago because she assaulted his mother, has been notified that unless he permits his wife to return he will be punished by White Caps.

ATLANTA, Ga., Dec. 21.—At Buchanan, Ga., half a dozen young men imitated the White Caps and attacked the house of a woman of easy virtue. A negro employed at the house remonstrated, when the attacking party beat and shot him to death.

Atlanta Constitution: What a raw day Wednesday was! How it blew and bit and chilled and stung us—and how bleak last night was, with its roaring and whistling and icy winds! You remember? Well, on yesterday a little girl, hugging a thin shawl about her shoulders, her bare legs literally blue with cold, rang the door bell of a comfortable residence—from her shivering lips came a plea for money to buy coal for her mother, who was sick. The money was furnished and an investigation made. In a miserable hut, through which the icy wind blew and whistled—huddled over the fireplace sat a woman—old as your mother or ours, sick and half starving. She had crawled from her bed, wrapped the single quilt about her stricken body, stuck her bare feet in the handful of ashes that still held some of the warmth of the fire. There she sat, fighting against freezing, sick and desperate, rubbing the fast-cooling ashes over her poor old feet.

South Boston, VA. July 27.—In the neighborhood of Meadsville, a quiet little village about ten miles from Halifax Courthouse, lives the family of Mr. R. C. Dodd. He is held in high esteem by his neighbors and the community generally. Wednesday night the 25th instant he was absent at a neighbor's house, expecting to go to Charlotte next day. He left his wife and children at home. Mrs. Dodd retired early and was aroused from her sleep about 1 o'clock by the presence of a negro man in her bedroom. He had raised the window of the room and before she was awakened was on her bed attempting the fiendish purpose that controlled him. An awful struggle, took place, the lady all the time making heartrending screams for help. The man, who worked for Mr. Dodd, occupied an out-house on the lot, and with him that night were his brother and two other negroes. He left his companions in his night-clothes, and, as stated, entered the room through the window. Mrs. Dodd's struggles and screams were so prolonged and desperate that her assailant finally became frightened and ran out of the front door of the house, but came around to Mrs. Dodd's window and asked why she was screaming. The other negro men then came up.

THE ARREST.

Yesterday morning a negro named Bruce Younger was arrested for the crime. He was fully identified by Mrs. Dodd, and was immediately brought to Halifax Courthouse and put in jail. Late yesterday evening it was rumored on the streets here and at Halifax Courthouse that Younger would be lynched by indignant citizens from Meadsville and throughout the county.

The officials of the county, of course, heard of the rumor and at once began to consider how to prevent the proposed lynching. They were met by the troublesome fact that there was no place the prisoner could be securely confined in, and as their every movement was watched they feared to take the negro from the jail because he might be rescued by his friends and a terrible affray between
confined in, and as their every movement was watched they feared to take the negro from the jail because he might be rescued by his friends and a terrible affray between white and colored people he precipitated. It was therefore deemed best to place a guard at the jail, but in this also great difficulty was experienced.

WERE SCARCE.

All the young men of the village were said to be at a dance; at any rate none could be found. Indeed, all the men of the town seemed to have vanished. Finally, however, Sheriff Moore succeeded in pressing into service six or seven gentlemen, who could not escape him, and they waited at the jail for further developments.

AT MIDNIGHT.

At about midnight a party of horsemen reached the jail. They at once demanded the keys, which the sheriff refused. Every man of the party seemed to have a pistol in his hand flashing and glittering in the moonlight. The party then issued orders for the court-yard, in which the jail is situated, to be cleared, which was speedily done, the sheriff and his squad being completely helpless and overpowered. The men went about their work with great deliberation, for the yard was picketed all around with guards, while another force with a pick broke open the jail and commanded Younger to come out.

PROTESTED INNOCENCE.

The man refused and protested his innocence again and again. Pistols were placed at his breast and he then consented. Younger, with a handkerchief tied over his mouth, was finally brought out by his captors, who at once proceeded down towards Foot's creek, a few hundred yards from the town. Reaching there they told the man his last hour had come, and gave him five minutes in which to pray. Still protesting his innocence he knelt down upon the bank of the creek, and in the still, ghostly moonlight, the scene was one of intense awe and solemnity—the prisoner preparing to meet his terrible death, his executioners standing around grim, silent, and determined.

When the doomed man had finished his prayer a rope was placed around his neck and he was led upon the foot-bridge (about twelve feet high) that spans the creek. He was told that he must die and was urged to confess his guilt.

CONFESSION.

At the last moment he did so, saying that he was the guilty man, and that Mrs. Dodd's statement (which I have given above) was entirely correct. He said that while he had not accomplished the object of his assault he had entered Mrs. Dodd's room with that intention and had used every effort to succeed, and was only prevented by her struggles and screams and the fear that he would be discovered.

DROPPED OFF.

Everything being ready he was dropped from the bridge, but the fall being a very short one his neck was not broken.

MANY SHOTS.

The party then fired their pistols at him at short distance time and again, and the shots rang sharp and clear upon the midnight air. Younger's body hung from the bridge until this morning, when it was cut down and carried to the court-house room, where your correspondent saw it this morning.

The man's clothing was scorched and burned in several places from the fire of the pistols, and about twenty-five or thirty bullets took effect. His face was not disfigured. This is the first lynching that ever occurred in this county, and considering the circumstances it was the most quiet affair of the kind recently reported. Everybody, black as well as white, seems to think that the wretch met a deserved fate, and some of the severest denunciations of him I have heard have been from men of his own color.

LITTLE CONCEALMENT.

The party who did the work were not masked. Some slight attempts were made, but were very feeble. Very little attempt was made to conceal their features. It was made up of men from different parts of the county, and there was an entire absence of excitement or passion.

The act was but the swift vengeance of an outraged people. They met about two miles from Halifax Courthouse and held a full consultation, and it was determined that if the negro persisted in his innocence to the bitter end that the rope would be cut and he would be taken back to jail. He was only to be killed if he confessed.

Mrs. Dodd, at the time of the assault, was in a very delicate condition, and was terribly frightened and bruised and injured. At this writing it is feared she may not survive the shock. Indeed, it is reported that she died this morning.

HALIFAX COURTHOUSE, VA., July 27.—Editor Times: Early yesterday morning Bruce Younger (colored), was committed to jail charged with the hemious crime of rape upon Mrs. Robert Dodd, a white married lady, wife of a respectable farmer living near Meadsville. While the act was hellish enough, it was made doubly so by the ladies peculiar condition. Some time after midnight last night about one hundred men rode into town and secured their horses on the out side of the Court-house square, and proceeded to the jail. Globe-Democrat: For several months past the stockmen owning cattle in the southern part of De Soto county, south Florida, have been suffering from the depredations of a well-organized band of cow thieves, who make their headquarters in Lee county, nearly opposite Fort Myers. The marks and brands of hundreds of beef cattle were changed and then driven to Myers and Punta Rassa, where they were sold to parties buying for the Key West market. The eattlemen received information from parties in Myers that cattle with bloody ears and poorly disguised brands were being brought to that market for sale by the Corbett brothers, who, it seems, were the leaders in this wholesale steal.

Ropes were placed around the necks of the three Corbetts, and the enraged cattlemen were for at once pulling them over the limb of a convenient water oak. A GRANT COUNTY WAR.
A County Seat Contest Leads to More Trouble—Ulysses and Appomattox at War.

GARDEN CITY, Kan., Oct. 19.—Latest reports from Grant County are that Ulysses received a clear majority of 2,150 over all competitors at the county seat election Tuesday. The rival towns were Ulysses, Appomattox, Golden, Shockeyville and Spurgeon.

The residents of Appomattox accuse General T. T. Taylor and Colonel J. A. Grayson, of Hutchinson, who are members of their town company and who managed the campaign for them, of selling them out, and a mob of irate citizens captured them and threatened them with violence, but the sheriff and a posse rescued them.

Colonel Grayson, who was in this city yesterday, said that the Appomattox and Ulysses town companies entered into articles of agreement that no "boodle" should be used, the forfeit in case of violation to be $10,000. About three o'clock on election day, it is alleged, the Ulysses people commenced using their money lavishly to buy votes. This so enraged the Appomattox people that they at once seized General Taylor and Colonel Grayson and put them under guard. Threats of lynching were freely made and they were forced to assign to the leaders of the mob the agreement with the Ulysses Town Company, and to give warranty deeds to all the property they owned in Appomattox or elsewhere. Not content with this, checks aggregating $60,000 on every bank in which the two were supposed to have money were presented, and the prisoners signed them without a murmur. They made written acknowledgment at the suggestion of the mob that their action was of their own free will. At night, guarded by nine friends, they went to Hartland, where they boarded the train.

Payment of all the checks has been stopped by telegraph and proceedings will be commenced to set aside the deeds they signed at the "request" of their captain. General Taylor is now at Larkin while Colonel Grayson has gone to Hutchinson. They consider themselves lucky to have escaped with sound necks.

It is thought the mob has gone on to Ulysses to make an attempt to collect the $10,000 forfeit and war is feared.

DELTA, DELTA COUNTY, COLORADO, TUESDAY, OCTOBER 30, 1888.
A Kansas Experience.
TOPEKA, Kan., Oct. 24.—General Thomas Taylor of Hutchinson, a prominent gubernatorial candidate in the late Republican convention and a member of the Legislature, had a thrilling and starling experience last week in the town of Appomattox, Grant county. The distinguished gentleman was for two days held a prisoner by an infuriated mob and very narrowly escaped being lynched.

General Taylor was one of the founders of the town of Appomattox, being President of the Appomattox Town Company, and A. Grayson of Hutchinson, secretary. Three miles east of Appomattox is the town of Ulysses. The two villages have been very bitter enemies ever since they were organized. An election was held last Friday to choose a county seat for Grant county. It was an exciting contest between the two towns, which were of about equal strength. After the election it was found that Ulysses was ahead.

By some means the people of Appomattox got it into their heads that Mr. Taylor and Mr. Grayson had sold out to their rival the condition being that for a certain number of lots in the winning town the defeated town should unite their interests with the successful one. This meant a heavy loss to a great many property owners in Appomattox, and they were up in arms. In a very short time a hundred men heavily armed gathered at the Appomattox hotel, where Taylor and Grayson were staying and compelled them at the point of a pistol to surrender. They were handled very roughly and threats were freely made that they would be hanged up. The two men were closely guarded and it is reported that they were compelled to give their checks for a large sum of money in settlement of various supposed claims for damages.

After two days of imprisonment the gentlemen secured their liberty by a very unique plan. A party of their friends went to the hotel and by pretending that they came for the purpose of mobbing the prisoners, attracted the attention of the guards, thus giving the two men an opportunity to escape from an upper window. A carriage was in waiting near by and General Taylor and Mr. Grayson were quickly driven to Loken, the nearest railroad point. The mob surrounding the hotel did not discover that their prisoners had escaped until they were some distance out of town and it was too late to stop them. They arrived in this city this afternoon and declare that they had a very fortunate escape.

There is great excitement at Russell Springs, Logan county, Kansas, over the discovery of a very rich deposit of nickel. A number of claims have been staked out and there is a general rush for that point. The discovery was made by two prospectors, Jerome Eldron and Clinton Phelps. It is in what is termed a blanket ledge, cropping out all along the gulch, and is so situated that it can be mined with a pick and shovel and wheelbarrow. No shafts will be sunk and no tunnels run, and the cost of mining will be merely nominal. As soon as they made the discovery they sent specimens to the assaying offices in Denver, Kansas City and Topeka, to the United States mint at Philadelphia, and to assayers in other cities. These assays ran from 2 to 25 per cent. pure nickel. Nickle is worth $16 per ounce. Thus it will be seen that at the lowest estimate this deposit is worth $70,000 per ton. It is reported that the two prospectors have been offered $50,-000 for their bonanza.

PHILLIPS, Wis., July 15.—An outrage was committed by a father here that has been seldom equaled in the state, and one which was followed by summary punishment by rightly indignant citizens. For some time past Gust Johnson, a homesteader, has been punishing his 10-year-old boy in a most inhuman manner for some trifling misdemeanors. Last Sunday morning Johnson, who lives in the township of Worcester, tied the youth to a post with a log chain and flogged him to a point where death would have been preferable. The little prisoner was not released after the flogging, but left to suffer from his wounds until Monday night, when he succeeded in making his escape to the woods, where he roamed about until Wednesday night without food or shelter. He was found by a Wisconsin Central station crew nearly famished and exhausted with hunger, and as frightened as a wild animal. He reported his father's cruelty to the crew, and, with other indignant citizens, they waited upon Johnson Thursday night, and, with a rope, proceeded to string him up to the limb of a tree, but he begged so hard and pitifully and promised so faithfully never to whip the boy again that he was lowered to the ground, and, after receiving a sound threshing, marched to the railway tank, and was given a cold bath.

It has since come to light that Johnson has been in the habit of tieing his son with a lock and chain for weeks at a time, feeding him on bread and water and administering a whipping every day. The boy is now being taken care of by the people of the settlement.

Tailbotton New Era: A good joke on one of Talbot's respectable farmers is going the rounds which, while it shows an eye to business is not without an amusing feature. The cows of this farmer Mr. A. got into the pea field of his neighbor, Mr. B. and destroyed, about ten bushels of peas. A Mob Attempts to Hang a Negro Prisoner in Grenada, But are Foiled by the Vigilance of our Officers.
"A colored man named Henry Johnson was brought into town Thursday charged with attempting to commit an assault upon the person of a young white lady a few miles south of town the night before. The committing trial was set for Friday morning and an immense crowd was present to hear the testimony, only a small portion of which was taken, however, that of the young lady and a portion of Mr. Smith's, the gentleman who made the arrest, when the attorney for the defence waved further examination and asked for bail. The morning express came just at the time, and it was evident to the onlookers that it was only a scheme to get the prisoner forwarded at once to the county jail at Coffeeville. It worked, too, and despite the clamors for a trial and the taking of all the testimony the prisoner was hurried to the train, put aboard and safely conveyed out of town. We cannot refrain from saying that his safe removal was the strongest indication of the law and other loving nature of these people this section has ever known. The proof against the prisoner was not conclusive by any means. Had it been there is no power on earth could have saved him from the hands of the father and brothers present, but it is too seldom that judgment is given away, the passions are inflamed at the bare thought of such a crime and nothing is known but hanging. We congratulate the people upon the control of their passions. Wait until the prisoner is found guilty and then there will be no one to say nay."

The above we clip from the Water Valley Progress, of August 4th. Instead of taking the above colored prisoner to Coffeeville, Sheriff Cox, of Yalobusha county, brought him to Grenada for safe keeping, on the 12 o'clock train on Friday of last week. The same night a crowd of at least one hundred citizens of Water Valley came down on the 9 o'clock train, for the purpose of taking the prisoner out of our jail and hanging him. In the mean-time our officers got an intimation of their coming, and swiftly spirited the prisoner away to an adjoining county, where was he safely lodged in jail. On the arrival of the Water Valley crowd at the depot, they were met by our Mayor, Sheriff and police officers, who informed them that the prisoner was not here, and they were commanded to desist from all violence and unlawfulness. Nothing would satisfy the crowd until a committee among their number, was escorted through the jail by Sheriff Jones and Marshal Wright. They seemed to be very much disappointed at not finding their man, but left immediately for the depot, where they took the north-bound train for home, without doing any violence. With but few exceptions, the crowd was orderly and well-behaved, and seemed to have come on their business in a very systematic way. During the time the saloons, at the request of the Mayor, were closed, and all intoxicants kept away from the crowd.

The admission of the Progress as published above, shows that our officers were not only justified in giving the prisoner protection, but that it was due the prisoner himself, from the fact that "the proof against the prisoner was not conclusive by any means." A very large majority of our people feel that a great injustice was done Grenada, from the fact that if the man deserved hanging, he should have been hung at Water Valley, near where the offence was committed, and not throw the responsibility on our Sheriff, and the odium of mob violence upon our town and community. If such was their intention, it was nothing less than a high-handed outrage. We congratulate our Sheriff, Mayor and Marshals upon their prompt action in this matter.

WEST CHESTER, Pa., Nov. 21.—James Mills, the colored assailant and would-be murderer of Bertie Howard, the 11-year-old adopted daughter of Farmer Isaac Beck, residing near Paoli, was brought to West Chester yesterday and lodged in prison. He was captured in bed last night at Cranberry, N. J. The hack in which he was conveyed to prison was surrounded by a hooting mob.

On Thursday evening, Sept. 28, Bertie Howard was returning from school when she was met by the colored brute. He took her to a field and assaulted her. He then carried her to a neighboring pond and threw her in. She dragged herself to the bank and was again thrown back by Mills. This was repeated the third time. The girl then lay still in the water and the assailant, thinking she was dead, left. He went to his house, where he had been living with a white woman, changed his clothes and left. Bertie managed to drag herself from the water and to a neighboring house, where she was taken in and cared for. For several days it was thought she would die, but she finally began to mend.

Mills acknowledged committing the assault, but says he was drunk at the time. He denies, however, that he attempted to drown the girl.

BERTIE HOWARD'S ESCAPE
The people of Hightstown, N. J., were greatly excited yesterday over the arrest there of James Mills, the negro who tried to drown Bertie Howard, the eleven-year-old adopted daughter of John Beck, near Paoli, Chester county, Pa. Two months ago the Hightstown people all read the Philadelphia papers, which gave long accounts of the crime at the time it was committed, and they are horrified to learn that the author of it had been living near there. For several days a couple of strangers had been nosing around Hightstown and making inquiries which led the folks to believe they were detectives. The strangers themselves did not tell who they were, but a little before 8 o'clock yesterday morning they turned up at the Pennsylvania Railroad depot in Hightstown with James Mills in their custody. All the explanation made of the arrest was that given to the baggage master. They said they had captured Mills at the house of a farmer named Clayton, who lived near Englishtown, about seven miles east.

The farmer owned a threshing machine and Mills was one of his helpers. They said they had tracked Mills from Paoli when he fled through the woods at the time the country side was up in arms after him, to Media, Pa., thence through northern and eastern Pennsylvania, northern New Jersey into Connecticut, and then to New Brunswick, whence Mills came to the neighborhood of Hightstown. He had been here about two weeks when the detectives found him. The detectives say that Mills admitted his identity and guilt, and was willing go back to Paoli without a requisition. The detectives left with him on the 8 o'clock train for Philadelphia.

There is a reward of $500 for his arrest, $250 offered by the friends of the girl assaulted and $250 by the authorities of Chester county.

On Thursday, Sept. 28, when Bertie Howard was returning to her home from school about 4:30 o'clock in the afternoon, Mills seized her almost in sight of Beck's farm house, so near that the family heard her scream but did not know what the sound meant. He carried her into a corn field where he tried to assault her. There he kept her for some time, and then dragged her into a neighboring orchard, where he tied her hands behind her back. He kept her there until late in the evening, he threatening to kill her if she cried out. Afterward he muffled her head in her cloak, dragged her away to a pond and threw her in. The brave little girl, although only 11 years old, got out of the water. Again he threw her in and again she managed to get out. For the third time the villain endeavored to drown her. This time he pushed her so hard that she went clear across the little pond and struck the bank on the other side. He then went away, thinking her dead. After he had disappeared the girl, still with her hands tied behind her back, scrambled out of the water and made her way to a house in the neighborhood, where she was kept all night. The next day, and for days afterward, the whole country side was scoured by men hunting for Mills, but he managed to elude them all.

West Chester, Pa., Nov. 20.—The negro brute, James Mills, who a few weeks ago assaulted and tried to drown Bertie Howard, the adopted daughter of farmer Isaac Beck, residing near Paoli, is now safely housed in the Chester county prison. Officer Robert Jefferson of this place, and Constable Jackson of Coatesville, arrested Mills last night near Oranberry, N. J., and brought him to West Chester this afternoon. With some trouble they got him to the Chester county prison, being compelled to put Mills in a cab to get him safely through the crowd of incensed men who lined the way from the railroad station to the jail. This evening Mills was given a partial hearing by Squire Eupert; the testimony of Bertie Howard, the pretty little girl who was Mills' victim, was given, and Mills was again committed to jail.

Isaac Beck, Bertie's adopted father, went to the prison with a revolver in his pocket, intending to shoot Mills on sight. His friends, partly by persuasion and partly by force, got the revolver from him before Mills was brought in.

Mills, when arrested, acknowledged committing the assault, but says he was drunk at the time. He denies however, that he attempted to drown the girl.

On Thursday evening, September 28th, Bertie Howard was returning from school when she was met by the colored brute Mills. He dragged her into a field close by and assaulted her. He then dragged her body to a neighboring pond and threw her in. She dragged herself to the bank and was again thrown back by Mills. This was repeated the third time. The girl lay still in the water, and the assistant, thinking she was dead, left.

He went to his house, where he had been living with a white woman, changed his clothes and left. Bert e managed to drag herself from the water and to a neighboring house, where she was taken in and cared for. For several days it was thought that she would die, but she finally commenced to mend, and is now apparently healthy, though she has never been the bright, happy child she was before the assault.

Mills confessed his crime making the following statement:

I was very drunk when I met the little girl. I worked on the next farm and I lived with my wife, who is a white girl. I have one young child. I don't remember much, but I did assault her after dragging her in the woods and tying her hands behind her back. I threw her in the water and took her out once, and then my mind don't know what happened, I was so full of rum. Maybe I threw her in again or she might have rolled in herself. I ran away I don't know where, and I have traveled all over. Every man I saw I was afraid of, and I expected to be arrested.

He seemed perfectly unconcerned while making his confession.

JOHN BOWEN CAPTURED.
A Long and Tiresome Chase-An Interview With Him-What He Says of the Attempted Lynching.
A Long and Tiresome Chase—An Interview With Him—What He Says of the Attempted Lynching.

The Westminster correspondent of the Baltimore Sun, under date of June 24, says:

Deputy sheriff Tyler arrived on the 5 p. m. train yesterday, having in custody John Bowen, colored, who escaped from a lynching party at Union Bridge, Carroll county, on June 15. He was met in Union Bridge by Israel Zeiber, a former deputy sheriff, of this place, who returned with them to Westminster. The news of Bowen's capture spread rapidly, and quite a crowd gathered at the depot here. There was no excitement and no demonstration of any kind. Bowen was taken to the jail in a closed carriage and placed in charge of the sheriff. Deputy Tyler has been in search of him since Thursday, and followed him from Emmitsburg to Greencastle, Pa., and captured him yesterday morning sitting on a fence near that place. Bowen offered no resistance, but asked protection. While passing through Union Bridge very few persons knew of the arrest, and there were not many at the depot. Everything is quiet and no excitement whatever. Bowen is charged with brutally assaulting a colored woman and blind colored man.

He is about five feet eight inches in height, medium dark, with high receding forehead, prominent lower jaw and thick lips, and wears a constant smile on his countenance. He is said to be a man of considerable courage, but had some dread of passing through Union Bridge, where he thought a crowd might attack him while he was handcuffed and defenseless. He appears to be greatly relieved now that he is in the custody of the sheriff and has the thick walls of the jail around him. His counsel, Mr. I. E. Pearson, found it hard to convince him that there was danger to him in his giving bail and going at large. "Why," said he, "they cannot hang me after I give bail, can they? There is no law for that." "Yes," replied his counsel, "they might hang you without any law." "Oh, no," said Bowen, "they can't hang me without law." He evidently thought that the hanging at Union Bridge was by authority of the law.

In an interview held with Bowen to-day he made the following statement: "I was in Westminster on Thursday, the 14th, to consult Mr. I. E. Pearson who, advised me to go back to Union Bridge and give bail. I did so, and went back on the 8.20 p. m., train and went direct to Mr. Calvin Wentz's saloon to get him to go my bail. While there Constable Repp with a crowd came down and with drawn pistols arrested me. I never resisted an officer, and would never do so. I was always anxious to give myself up if I would be protected, but after my first arrest the officers took so little pains to save me from the mob that I considered my life would be endangered if I surrendered to the officers. Constable Repp put me in the lock-up. About one o'clock that night I heard the mob at the door, and was terribly frightened. Old man Milbury, father of the girl, had a rope. There were two or three 'coons' and a large crowd of whites. I recognized all, and can give their names. They said they were going to hang me. I said: 'Men, this is cowardly—give me a chance; I am an innocent man,' but they would not listen. They put a rope around my neck and choked me so I could hardly breathe. Milbury called out to the crowd, 'Are you all ready out there?' and a voice I recognized replied, 'Yes, bring him out.' None of the crowd at first wore masks, but afterwards some of them put handkerchiefs over their faces, so the people of the town could not recognize them. I resisted all I could, but they had the rope around my neck and were too many for me. They put me in a wagon and took me out to the tree. I struggled and begged all the time, but to no avail. All the way I could hear the men swearing at me and urging those in charge of me to hurry up. When they reached the tree, which stands in a field belonging to Mr. Granville Haines, near the town, most of the crowd drew back a few steps and stood on one side. Two or three others threw the rope over a limb. While they were getting ready they forgot in their hurry to tie my hands, and as they prepared to draw me up I slipped my thumbs under the hoose, and quick as a flash darted away from them, taking the crowd entirely by surprise. They never had me off my feet at all, and the story that I asked time to pray was not true. I could tell from the manner and conversation of the men that they were in dead earnest, and would not give me time for anything, and would never have let me down after once drawing me up. They were all greatly excited. There is a great feeling of spite against me in Union Bridge by some people, and they urged the men who had me in charge to hurry up the job. They made a mistake in not tying my hands, but I suppose they were so much excited they forgot to do it. It is all a lie about my talking to people and making threats of burning the town and killing people. I am not revengeful, and don't want to be revenged; only if I am to be punished for breaking the law, the Union Bridge people ought to be treated the same way. They tried to kill me, and I did not hurt any of them, and they are guiltier than I would be even if I had done what they accuse me of doing."

Bowen gave his counsel the names of the people who, he says, tried to lynch him, but refuses to make them public and says he does not want them punished. He says they were excited and he does not believe they would harm him after their anger cools off a little. He persistently denies having assaulted Ida Milbury and her blind companion, Jones, both of whom have recovered.

CHICAGO, April 10.—An employee of the Stanley Detective agency, named John T. Walck, was very nearly lynched yesterday by the employees of the distillery of H. F. Shufeldt & Co., who discovered him spying upon the business of the company in the interest of the whisky trust. Shufeldt's distillery is the only one in the city not in the trust, which, it is stated, has since its formation last August kept up a relentless warfare upon the Shufeldt company. Walck had been observed watching the teamsters delivering goods, and on being found in the distillery was seized by the men, forced under a huge beam, and was having a rope put round his neck preparatory to lynching when one of the proprietors of the distillery appeared on the scene and rescued the spy. After Walck had written a statement of spying operations he was suffered to depart. The employees of the distillery say they shall certainly hang the next spy they catch.

Shufeldt's distillery is the only one north of the Ohio river which does not belong to the whisky trust. March 30 he was seen to take the address of Ellison & Harvey, Richmond, Va., from a consignment of goods being shipped to that firm by Shufeldt. A few days afterward Ellison & Harvey received a communication from Corning & Co., of Peoria, who belong to the trust, saying that they would sell them gin at $1.15 per gallon. As the list price of that article at that time was $1.25, Shufeldt & Co. became convinced that the Whisky Trust was employing detectives to ascertain the names of their customers in order to undersell them and drive them out of business. This suspicion was confirmed by a member of the trust, who, they say, told them that they must either close up or be ruined—the old Standard Oil method of stopping competition. Without having the least idea that he was being watched, Wolck used every means in his power to get inside the distillery. He was as well known to the managers, however, as any of their workmen, and all his efforts were unavailing. The firm consulted their lawyers, and found that they could obtain no adequate legal redress from either Wolck or his employers. Early this morning the detective applied to Mr. Thomas Lynch, the junior partner, for a position in the distillery. Mr. Lynch asked him a few questions, and told him he could go to work. In the meantime the employees had been informed of the methods that were being used by the Whisky Trust, and their indignation knew no bounds. Wolck went into the distilling rooms and seated himself upon a barrel, waiting for the signal to go to work. His eyes roamed restlessly about the room. He read the labels on the barrels, and took out a note-book and jotted down the address of the consignees. "Boys," said a man, grasping Wolck by the shoulders, "this is a Whisky Trust spy."

With a howl of rage, the forty men sprang forward to a man. Wolck reached his hand behind him and attempted to draw a revolver. In a second he was sprawling upon the floor, with his weapon in the possession of one of the workmen.

"No, you don't," shouted Mr. Lynch, standing over the prostrate man, with a murderous-looking "44" in his grasp.

"Hang the —— spy," shouted several men in a breath. A coil of half-inch rope was at once procured, and Wolck was securely tied "Now, —— you; you're goin' where the only trust is run by the devil."

The rope was tied around the neck of the trembling detective and one end thrown over a beam. Wolck turned pale and rolled his eyes in agony. "Don't kill me," he murmured; "I've got a wife and children. I didn't come here to play the spy, but to——"

At this juncture Mr. Lynch interfered and the rope was taken from Wolck's neck. He was firmly tied to a post, however, and it was with great difficulty that the men could be prevented from covering him with the slime from the distilling apparatus. On a promise of being released he consented to make a confession. A notary public was sent for and Wolck swore to a statement regarding the object of his visit. He claimed, however, that his main object was to see that there was no evasion of the internal revenue law on the part of Shufeldt & Co. After signing the confession, with a few parting kicks, the detective was sent into the street. SPY CAPTURED,
And Narrowly Escapes Summary Punishment.
The Whisky Trust Puts a Detective's Neck
in Jeopardy, and He Begs For
His Life.
Chicago, April 9.—The distillery of H. F. Shufeldt & Co., on Larrabee street, near Chicago avenue, is the only one north of the Ohio river that does not belong to the Whiskey Trust, and as a consequence the latter has waged an unceasing war upon it since August last, when the pool was formed. Detectives have been shadowing the distillery night and days and every shipment made by the house has been noted, Mossrs. Shufeldt & Co. having frequently received notice from their customers that rival hoops in the trust had agreed to sell their goods at from five to seven cents lower than Shufeldt's house possibly could. The distillery folks "got onto" the detective who was shadowing the house and found that he was John T. Walck, of Stanley's agency. This morning, to the great surprise of the distillery people, Walck applied for work and was readily given i. He was put to work in the warehouse, but had not been employed more than an hour when the men discovered who he was, and the greatest excitement reigned. "Kill him, string him up; don't let him out here alive," were the cries that resounded through the building, and it looked as though Walck's doom was sealed, for the men put him under a big beam, and were preparing to place a rope around his neck, when Thomas Lynch, a partner in the distillery interfered and saved him. The detective was then tied to a post by the rope it had been proposed to hang him with, and forced to tell the whole story. "For God's sake, spare me," he cried as the big tears rolled down his blanched cheeks. "I have a wife and two children; let me go, for their sakes." He said he had procured employment in the house for the purpose of finding out if the house was violating the revenue laws, and knew nothing of the Whiskey Trust. He was then allowed to go, but Mr. Lynch says the next dtective caught in the house will be hanged i.

A SPY NEARLY HANGED. A Whisky Trust Detective Ill-Used by Angry Workmen.
by Angry Workmen.

The only distillery in Chicago that is outside the whisky "Trust" is that of H. F. Shufeldt & Co. Ever since the formation of the Trust last August it has waged bitter warfare on the Shufeldt firm to force them to come into the fold. To help this on the Trust hired J. T. Wolck, a private detective, to watch the firm and obtain the addresses of their customers. The object of his work was ascertained by the firm, when Ellison & Harvey, of Richmond, Va., wrote Shufeldt & Co. that they had been offered gin at six cents per gallon less than they sold it at by a Trust distillery.

A lawyer was consulted, but the firm found that they had no legal redress against the spy or his employers. Wolck, who had been hanging around the distillery trying to get access to it on all sorts of pretenses, finally asked one of the partners for employment as a workman. He was readily engaged, but the other workmen were informed who he was. The spy had just pulled out his note-book to copy the shipping directions on some barrels, when forty workmen surrounded him yelling, "Hang the spy." Wolck made an effort to draw a revolver, but he was knocked down and disarmed, besides receiving numerous kicks. A rope was then thrown around his neck, and the workmen would have lynched him, had not the distillery proprietors interfered. Wolck begged for mercy and agreed to tell all he knew if he was only let go. The workmen tied him to a post and a notary public was sent for to whom Wolck made a statement giving the names of his employers. Then the workmen kicked him out into the street and as he fled showered stones after him.

Pranks of Some Raw Recruits Sent to Capt. Harris in the Park.
LIVINGSTON, August 29.—A batch of sixteen recruits was recently sent from Fort Keogh to Capt. Harris at the Mammoth Hot Springs. They have turned out to be about as tough a gang as were ever together. Six of them are now in the guard house for quite serious offenses. Three have deserted within the past few days. One was shipped back to Fort Keogh last week to be court martialed for some serious military offense. Yesterday one of them got drunk and attempted to run the hotel at the springs, refusing to obey the officer, and was only forced into camp at the muzzle of a six-shooter.

Ranchers Lynched.
HOLBROOK, Ariz., August 18.—Outlaws in Pleasant Valley lynched Wm. Nagler and Louis Nagler, ranchers and stockmen and unoffensive citizens. This is a continuation of the Tonto Basin or Pleasant Valley feud, which started one year ago in a scheme to drive out ranchmen and others holding interests detrimental to sheep owners. W. H. McRaigy, an employee of the Aztec Land and Cattle Company at the station at the foot of the Nogolen mountains, has just arrived and reports that he was ordered to leave the ranch. Those who have worked with him and know him best, speak well of him—say that he was quiet, sober and peaceable, and was never engaged in any questionable transactions to their knowledge.

Stott is a man who has made enemies and friends. His enemies say that he was a bad man—that he was the head and brains of a desperate gang of rustlers; while his friends say that he was an honest, honorable and deserving man.

From what meagre information we have been able to gather, this appears to be rather a high handed move, to say the least. We could hear of no charge whatever against Scott, who had gone to Pleasant Valley after a horse he had loaned to Neglin Bros., while he was waiting to hear from parties to whom he had written seeking employment. Wilson is in a similar position—no charges against him that we could hear of. If the lynchers had any charge against either, they did not make them known.

We are informed there was bad blood existing between Stott and Houck, over some charges Houck had made against him, and at one time, in Holbrook, Stott had told Houck in pretty plain language what he thought of him, winding up by telling Houck that if he wanted to make a fight of it, "to go and heel himself."

These making war on settlers who have fled their homes for self-protection, so far as we are informed, are generally not identified with the section of the country where the demon of digcord has obtained a footing. Quirks and quiddities of the law, alibies, changes of venue, hung juries and executive clemency will be invoked, and it is to this uncertainty in the administration of justice that the woods are full of outlaws whose chief reliance is in the virtue of gun powder, a protecting rock, a tree, a dense thicket. The latter were large stock men and have been in that country only a year or two. They came from Colorado, are Germans by birth, and before settling in Tonto Basin were considered hard-working, upright citizens, and we doubt if any one can truthfully say that they know the Neglin Bros. to be dishonest. Not Lynched.
The report that the Neglin brothers were lynched in Pleasant valley about a week ago, is not correct. At least, one of the brothers, Willian, is alive and well, the News editor having had the pleasure of an introduction to him to-day. However, it is barely possible that the other brother, Louie, has fallen a victim to the mob of Tonto Basin neck stretchers, although there is no apparent reasonable foundation for excuse for such an unlawful action, as it is understood the Neglin boys are peaceable and law abiding citizens.

Mr. Neglin arrived in Winslow yesterday from his ranch, located at the upper end of Pleasant Valley, which place he and his brother, Louie, left on about the 20th inst. for this place. Arriving at a point about eight miles this side of their ranch, the two brothers separated, Louie leaving the main trail to visit the ranch of a Frenchman a few miles off the road, with whom he had some business, requesting his brother to ride along slow until he should overtake him again. This the latter did for several hours, but finally conclude that his brother had changed his mind about rejoining him and gone on to Payson, rode into Winslow, where he learned the news of his reported lynching.

In the meantime the report of the Tonto Basin lynching had reached the ears of another Neglin brother, Charles, who lives at Durango, Colorado. The latter at once telegraphed Constable McKenney, here, for particulars, who, not knowing anything to the contrary, corroborated the report, and the said brother is now on his way to Winslow.

William will remain here until Charles arrives from Colorado, when, if nothing is heard of the still missing brother, steps will at once taken by them to instigate investigation.—Winslow News.

One Mexican Lynched and Another Dangerously Wounded.

Special to the Gazette.

CALDWELL, TEX., Jan. 16.—Saturday evening one of the Mexicans named Mat Pettis, in jail charged with the murder of old man Alford, which occurred about ten days ago near this place, made a confession of his guilt, in which he admitted that he did the killing and was assisted by another Mexican, one Reto. About $8.30 o'clock Saturday night the jail was approached by a mob of forty or fifty people and admission was demanded of the guards. The mob entered the jail at the front door and passing through a wooden partition entered the run-around of the cages. The Mexicans were located in a cage with a third Mexican and one negro. Shooting began at once and after the mob left the Sheriff and others entered and found the Mexican, who admitted his guilt, dead, having been shot four times. The Mexican who was implicated and who also made a confession was shot and is dangerously wounded. The other Mexican and the negro were unhurt.

A COMPLETE MYSTERY.
Part of the Money Stolen from the Panola County Treasurer's Office Recovered. Correspondence of the Gazette.

CARTHAGE, TEX, Feb. 14.—The mnrder and robbery of County Treasurer D. C. Hill remains a complete mystery. A young white man was arrested on suspicion, but released, as there was no evidence whatever against him. A colored barber was arrested to-day, and is held pending investigation.

This evening there was a great deal of excitement in town on account of a part of the money having been found in a fence corner near town by some parties who were searching the woods near a vacant house. A shot sack containing $43 in silver, together with a school book of some kind with the name of D. C. Hill (the name of the murdered man) written in the back, showing conclusively that it was a part of the stolen money. Every thing is being done to hunt down the perpetrators of this terrible murder. The county will offer a large reward, and the citizens have offered a reward of $500 already, and will doubtless increase this. The Governor has been appealed to also to offer a reward.

A Thousand Silver Dollars Found Buried in a Negro Barber's Yard.
A Thousand Silver Dollars Found Buried in a Negro Barber's Yard. special to the Gazette.

LONGVIEW, TEX., Feb. 16.—Another and perhaps very important chapter has been added to the D. C. Hill, county treasurer, murder at Carthage. Our information is reliable and from two different sources. Day before yesterday a child was playing in the garden belonging to the house where a negro barber named George Tibet lived. This child found a silver dollar in the mound when search was instituted. By digging about one thousand silver dollars were found. All seemed to have been but lately and hastily buried. Tippet was then arrested and is in the Carthage jail. If any other evidence against this man is known our informants had not heard it.

George Tippet is a son of John Tippet, a well and favorably known negro man who has lived here a long time and has by his frugality and hard toil bought a lot and built quite a nice house and nothing wrong was ever known or suspected of the old man. His son is almost white and was raised here, but nothing wrong was ever known of him here, yet it is said he didn't bear a very good reputation or was thought by some to be a desperate and suspicious character—especially in this case from the very first, and now that the money has been found at his home it will seem very strong proof of his guilt. Considerable fears are entertained here of lynching the negro.

It is rumored that a white man is suspected as either accomplice or instigator of this crime, and this $1000 was the negro barber's share, or that the money being silver and unmanageable was planted, and this tell-tale dollar found by the child was to direct suspicion towards the already suspected negro in order to effectually hide the real murderers. Be it as it may, the people of Carthage will slit these clews to the very bottom, and the real murderer will soon be located beyond doubt.

Referring to the special from Austin, going the sounds of the press, about the probable amount of money stolen in this case being much less than was first supposed, the latest reports we have from Carthage show still larger losses, aggregating more than the $6000 first reported. This however is not official, as the books have not yet been fully balanced and all depositors heard from.

TREASUREK HILL'S MURDERER.
The Son of the Sheriff of Panola County
Confesses, Giving all the Details.
Special to the Gazette.

BECKVILLE, TEX., Feb. 28.—About noon yesterday Tom Forsyth, son of the Sheriff of Panola county, was arrested for the murder of County Treasurer Hill on February 10. Young Forsyth has been under suspicion since his finding the sack of silver near the yard of the negro barber, Tippett, and has been under close surveillance since. When arrested he is said to have endeavored to throw the crime on Tippett, but immediately afterwards weakened, saying: "No, he is innocent. No one had anything to do with it but myself."

He is said to have confessed that he committed the murder while court was adjourned for dinner. The details of the confession are said to be horrible in the last degree. The widow of the murdered treasurer is said to have lost her mind, and the mother of young Forsyth fell in the street upon hearing the crowd crying out that her son was arrested and was making a confession. Two of the best women in the county are thus plunged into a living death, and numerous relatives throughout the county are worse than horror-stricken. Forsyth is but twenty-two, and does not look like a villain.

All but $700 of the money has been recovered. Being so far from telegraphic facilities makes it impossible to get particulars.

ANOTHER ACCOUNT.

Special to the Gazette.

LONGVIEW, TEX., Feb. 28 —For several days officers and citizens have been secretly hard at work on the Panola county murder case, Thomas Forsyth being the suspected murderer of County Treasurer Hill on the 10 h inst. He was known to have gambled very freely with the construction crews on the new railway nearly completed to Carthage, losing as high as $200 in one night, and this money all bore the stain of blood on its face. Several of these blood-stained bills were proved beyond a doubt to have been in the treasury at the time of the murder and robbery, but on account of this young man's social standing his arrest was deferred till the last possible moment, or till the evidence had piled up so high that nothing else could be done. The arrest was made as quietly as possible, but the fact flew like lightning and it was shouted so loud through the streets of the quiet little town that Forsyth's mother heard that her son was arrested and had made a full confession, the details of which are said to be horrible in the extreme. Mrs. Forsyt fell swooning on the streets apparently losing her mind, while at the home of the murdered County Treasurer, it is said, his widow has become a hopeless maniac. Young Forsyth is scarcely twenty-one years of age, and has acted as deputy sheriff for his father for seven or eight years, having the esteem and confidence of all who knew him. The only part of his confession known here is that he killed Treasurer Hill at noon Friday while the court had adjourned for dinner. It will be remembered that young Forsyth was the man who found the money buried near the residence of the negro barber Tippett who, he now says, had nothing to do with the murder or robbery. Great apprehension is felt for the safety of young Forsyth against mob law, but as his father is sheriff, it is likely with the assistance of 100 sworn deputies, he may be saved till he is moved to a place of safety, which is the plan suggested. Nearly all the stolen money was recovered. Owing to the absence of wire, and only one mail each day, but few particulars are obtainable.

LYNCH LAW.

Forsyth, Murderer of Treasurer Hill, Hanged by a Mob of 400 Men.

The Villain Begged Piteously Not to be Killed by Being Burned.
LONGVIEW, February 29.—Last night, while the news of the arrest of Tom Forsyth and his confession of the murder and robbery of D. C. Hill, treasurer of Panola county, was being flashed over the wires from this place, quite another scene was being enacted in Carthage, which has no telegraphic connections. About 400 men were taking out of the jail, by force, young Forsyth, who offered no resistance, but begged only to be spared death by fire. He climbed up a ladder while both of his hands were behind him, and, at the word, jumped off, breaking his neck, and dying at the end of the rope. All this was done quicker than it takes to record it. No masks were used, and the bright moonlight, at 10 o'clock p. m., shone as bright as day, disclosing the familiar features of about 400 of Panola county's best citizens. The scene was in the court yard, right in plain sight of the hotel veranda. After life was extinct he was cut down and carried by the lynchers to the very spot still stained with the blood of County Treasurer D. C. Hill, and laid down in a similar position, and the mob then quietly dispersed, and friends took the young man's remains and prepared them for the coffin. His body was taken to Beckville for interment. He confessed to Mr. H. E. Parker, who worked up the case. Mr. Parker's first suspicion was aroused when he took young Forsyth to the spot where Treasurer Hill was murdered, and from that time on he left nothing undone to find out where the money was concealed. He first succeeded in getting Forsyth to believe he was after the negro barber, Tippett, thereby turning all suspicion. He brought young Forsyth up to his place ostensibly to shadow Tippett, whose father lives here. While here, young Forsyth gambled, and, being broke, borrowed money from Parker, which he paid back at Carthage when he returned. The young man continued to lose and replenish from the stolen monoy, each visit to which was closely watched until the whereabouts of the money was located. Mr. Parker, wishing to locate the silver, which Forsyth never seemed to resort to, asked him if he couldn't get him some silver, as he could not raise any in town, to which Forsyth assented, and soon was shadowed to a thicket in the wood near Carthage. After some search a broken pine limb was found, under which fresh dirt was discovered. Upon digging the money was found and guarded, then further developments were awaited until Monday, when the arrest was made, and the lynching was deferred by young Forsyth's confession in open court. The money was found in Forsyth's trunk in his room at his father's. He said he killed Treasurer Hill at noon, while no one else was at the court house and buried the money in an old house near by, and rode out in the country to see a young lady that evening. Returning late he took the bills to his room and buried the silver as stated above.

The scene throughout the entire section beggars description. Everybody is up in arms to protect themselves and their property, and the greatest excitement prevails.

The jail at Pikeville, containing eleven of the captured men of Hatfield's party, is guarded by sixteen armed men, day and night, and pickets are sent out every night in all directions from the town to prevent a surprise and rescue.

So far seven of the McCoy gang have been killed and two wounded, while the Hatfields have had nine killed, five wounded and eleven captured.

BORDER VENDETTA.
THE HATFIELD SIDE OF THE LOGAN
COUNTY WAR.

Killed—The Kentucky Gang

Special Telegram to the Register.
CHARLESTON, W. VA., January 25. — To-day's mail brings more information from Logan county concerning the trouble growing out of the Hatfield-McCoy trouble in Pike county, Ky., and Logan county, W. Va. Senator J. B. Floyd received a letter from Logan Court House this evening, from his brother, which fully explains the erroneous account of the last fight between the Kentucky outlaws and the West Virginia officers, which occurred Saturday last. It was not the Hatfield gang, as the Enquirer of the 24th has it, who was concerned in the fight, but a posse of men armed with the authority of the law, through the Sheriff of Logan county, who had made a raid on the Kentucky gang, who were known and charged with the late murder of old man Vance on West Virginia soil. It must be remembered those outlaws had

INVADED WEST VIRGINIA SOIL, bent upon murder and destruction.

The writer of the letter was a member of the posse of the Logan county officers, and knows what he is writing about. The letter is under date of January 22, 1888. Governor Wilson has been in telegraphic communication with Governer Buckner, of Kentucky, and it is likely if some steps are not taken by the Kentucky government to prevent further invasion by the crowd from Pike county, the Governor of this State will deem it necessary to adopt some means for the protection of the people of Logan county.
Mr. Floyd's Correspondent Says:
"We are about to get into a war with the Kentucky gang who killed James Vance some days ago. Warrants are issued for the arrest of some six of the gang who committed the murder and were placed in the hands of Constable J. R. Thompson to be executed and he summoned a guard of thirteen men to make the arrests. We were over the mouth of Grapevine, in this county, and there we were fired upon by about thirty men with Winchester rifles. We were in an open field and the balls just hailed around us until we charged on them. When the firing began Henry Thompson and I were in front on our horses. We all jumped from our horses and returned the fire with our Winchesters and the firing kept up for about thirty minutes, when we started for some trees about 175 yards away.
At this time they fired another volley and killed one of our men, Wm. Dempsey, shooting him three times. They were behind a fence all the time and we could see nothing but the heads of their gang.

BUD M'COY WAS KILLED
and another man was wounded whose name I do not know. They all had Winchester rifles and said they had started to Logan C. H. to take Elias Hatfield and burn the town. Three of their horses were killed during the fight. You must go and see the Governor at once and have a stop put to those desperadoes coming over here and killing men and robbing them after they are killed. The people of the county are going to hold a moss meeting here to marrow, asking the Governor to send men over to put a stop to this thing. If the State would furnish us a hundred Winchesters and plenty of ammunition we would not need the men. See the Governor as soon as you get this and let us know what can be done. I can tell you that I heard many a Winchester ball pass my head. It is almost a young war over here. People are laying out from their homes on account of those Kentucky desperadoes. See to this matter at once and let me hear from you. [Signed] W. P. FLOYD.

State of West Virginia, Executive Department, Charleston, January 26, 1888.

Sir: Since my telegram of yesterday, I have positive information that William Dempsey was killed, last Thursday, in Logan county, this State, while acting as a deputy, under the authority of a warrant for the arrest of Frank Phillips and others for the murder of James Vance, by a party of thirty or forty men from Kentucky, armed with Wilchester rifles.

My information is of the most trustworthy character that Vance had been waylaid but a short time before, in Logan county, by twenty-three armed men from Kentucky, led by Phillips, and murdered in the most brutal manner.

Warrant was sued out and placed in the hands of a constable, for the arrest of Phillips and others. The constable, on hearing that the Phillips band were in Logan county, summoned a posse of thirteen, including Dempsy, to assist in making the arrest. While the posse were on the search for the parties named in the warrant they were fired upon by the Phillips marauders and Dempsy was killed.

Origin of the Feud.

From what I can learn, this feud dates back to the early years of the late war—the Hatfields and McCoys representing opposite sides of the service—and commenced by the shooting of one of the Hatfields by the McCoys. It was limited to those two families, and ended by the killin of one of the Hatfields and three of the McCoys, in 1881 or 1882. Recently the hope of reward has prompted a set of men, quite as lawless as either the Hatfields or McCoys, to the commission of heinous crimes against the laws of this State, and upon its citizens while discharging their duty as officers of the law.

CHAPTER IX. RAIDING THE HATFIELDS.
The murder of Allaphare roused Pike county as it had not been roused since the civil war. The mountaineers have chivalry if not courage, and they were ready, after a fashion, to avenge the murder of a woman. Out of a host of volunteers Frank Phillips selected twenty-three men, and early on the morning of Jan. 6 rode out of Pikeville to raid Logan county for indicted Logan Regulators. They reached Anse Hatfield's home, on the bank of Tug River, opposite the mouth of Peter Creek, at night. Of course Anse was not at home, but the women and children were, and they were terribly alarmed. Jim McCoy and five others stayed there that night, one keeping guard all the time, of course.

Next morning very early the mob went down to Thacker Creek, where Shang Ferrall lives, and took him along to prevent him from giving an alarm. Three miles up above Thacker lived Uncle Jim Vance, but when they reached the house no one was there. It is a remarkable fact that a trail of blood from the burned home of Old Randall led down to Tug River, was found again on the east side, and ended at Jim Vance's yard. The Kentuckians were able to trace the trail on the 6th quite easily.

From Vance's the mob started to go over on Mate Creek, following up a branch that was a shorter way than the regular road. At the head of the branch, and right in the gap of the

mountain, they met old Mrs. Vance coming down with an empty pail in her hand. She had been carrying breakfast up to Uncle Jim, and to Cap, who had slept in that mountain. As she saw the mob she turned and shouted:

"Here they come."

"How many?" asked Uncle Jim.

"About forty. I reckon."

During this talk the Kentuckians had charged up past the woman.

Uncle Jim yelled "Halt!" and then shouted, "Charge 'em, boys! Rally, boys! Charge 'em!" and at the same time began to shoot.

The orders, except the first, were bluff, for there were no boys there to rally, except Capt. Hatfield, who flunked and ran like a sheep with dogs after it. He did not even shoot one shot. But Uncle Jim was too old to run, and made a virtue of necessity. He dodged behind a locust stub still several feet high and eight inches thick, and, taking aim at Frank Phillips, who led the mob, fired. Phillips is a remarkably cool-headed desperado. Just as the old man got his gun to his face Phillips dropped to the ground, and the bullet passed harmlessly over his head. Then he jumped up and fired as he ran forward to gain the shelter of a tree; but the old man fired again, and again Phillips dodged. This seems almost incredible, but the story is told by both parties. After this shot Phillips gained the shelter of a big oak, and tried to get a shot at the old man from it. As he peered around, he saw the old man had the drop on him and dodged back just in time. The bullet knocked a shower of bark into Phillips's face. But at this same instant Phillips levelled his gun and fired square at the centre of the stump that concealed the old man. The stump was partly rotten, and the ball passed through it, striking Uncle Jim's cartridge belt and knocking him away from his shelter. Before the old man could recover himself Phillips had pumped in a fresh cartridge and shot him through the body. Uncle Jim dropped to the ground behind a log, and Phillips ran forward, supposing the old man was done for. In truth he was fatally hurt, but he was game yet. He had drawn a revolver as he fell, and before Phillips had taken two steps he saw the old man peering over the log holding the pistol with both hands. Uncle Jim was afflicted with a sort of St. Vitus dance that made his eyes roll and his whole frame shake about, yet he was accounted the best pistol shot in Logan county. Phillips dropped the moment he saw the old man, and the old man shrunk down a bit too. That was a mistake, for it enabled Phillips to aim his rifle where the old man's head must appear as he raised to look for Phillips. In a moment the gray hairs on his forehead rose above the log and Phillips fired. The ball knocked the old man's hat ten feet away and scattered his brains over the leaves for a yard around. The old lady, his wife, saw him killed. Walking up to his body she said: "Pore ole man; he's dead," and then walked away. Uncle Jim had been neither a faithful nor a kind husband, and the widow shed no tears.

The killing of Uncle Jim ended that raid. The Kentucky mob did not develop a relish for blood. They returned to Kentucky, but on Jan. 9 started on another raid. This time they went on Beech Creek, in Logan county. They reached the house of Justice Wall Hatfield at noon, and leaping their horses over the fence, charged on the house. Wall, instead of jumping for his gun, ran to the door to see what was the racket (as he supposed) with the cows. Jim McCoy covered him with a rifle, and the Justice threw up his hands. In the house the mob found Doc and Sam Mayhorn, who were wanted for killing the three McCoy boys. This made three prisoners. The mob went on up the creek, however, and found Plyant Mayhorn and Andy Varny, and then went over on another branch and got L. D. McCoy. Andy Varny tried to escape, but Sam McCoy and Dave Stratton ran him down instead of shooting him, according to the custom.

The third and last raid was made beginning Jan. 16. There were thirty-three men in the mob. On the 18th they reached West Virginia, opposite Peter Creek, and rode down along the bank of Tug River to the mouth of Gravesine Creek. Here lived Cap Hatfield. Jim McCoy was in advance of the rest of the mob, who had to ride along single file, of course, on account of the road being narrow. His horse was restive, and when within a short distance of the creek Jim let it go ahead on the run. Rounding a little spur of the mountain, Jim found himself riding square at thirteen of the Logan Regulators, who were in Cap's yard, guns in hand, waiting for the Kentuckians. Jim tried to rein in his horse, but at that instant the Regulators began firing, and the beast danced with fear. The dancing probably saved Jim's life, for it prevented fair aim.

Now, although no one else was in sight, the Regulators knew that others were behind Jim, and so stepped off to one side, where they could get shelter behind a fence. Meantime Jim managed to get off of his horse and quiet the beast, although the bullets were whistling on all sides. Then Jim coolly laid his gun on the ground, pulled off his overcoat, which was

too tight for him, and, placing it on the saddle, turned the horse loose. Then he picked up his gun, walked deliberately to a fence corner, and, taking aim over it, fired. He brought his man down at the first shot. The man was Bill Dempsey. At that the other twelve Regulators turned and ran like sheep, with Cap Hatfield leading the way, although no other Kentuckian had come in sight save Budd McCoy, and he had been shot down by a bullet in his shoulder.

The Kentuckians gathered in Cap's yard, but could at first find no one there, although Jim, who did not go into the yard, had said he had shot one man. But a trail of blood was found that led into a shuck pen. There they found Bill Dempsey, shot through the body.

"What is your name?" said Frank Phillips.

"Bill Dempsey," said he, holding up his hands. "I am not armed, gentlemen, and am diving now. Please don't shoot me any more. Don't, don't."

The last words were uttered as he saw Phillips draw a revolver. Several of the mob saw the revolver, too, and jumped to catch it, but they were too late. Phillips shot the man through the head. That act ended the raiding business. It was especially bad for the Kentuckians, for Dempsey was there as a lawful police officer to arrest raiding parties.

But the raids had affected the Hatfields much as the deeds of the Regulators had previously affected the McCoys, only worse. They immediately abandoned their farms and moved over to Island Creek, in the neighborhood of Logan Court House, and here they are now. Jonce

FOUR LYNCHINGS IN KANSAS. The Citizens Disgusted by the Law's Leniency Toward Murderers.
KANSAS CITY, June 28.—A mob at Minneapolis, Kan., took Chubb McCarthy, murderer of Mike Dorsey, from jail early this morning and hanged him to a tree. This was the last of four lynchings in the State within twenty-four hours. The others were Wallace Mitchell, who was strung to a telegraph pole at Syracuse, and John Risbee and Wyley Lee, negroes, who died together at Chetopa. The State law in Kansas in relation to capital punishment is a peculiar one. According to the statutes, a person convicted of murder in the first degree is sent to the penitentiary for one year, and at the expiration of the period is liable to be hanged at any time the Governor sees fit to sign the death warrant. No Governor has ever signed a warrant under such circumstances, and as a result there are fifty-four murderers under sentence of death in the State prison. To-day's record is the logical outcome of the situation.

About two weeks ago Wallace Mitchell assassinated a man and boy at Syracuse. He escaped to Colorado, but was captured and brought back on Tuesday. He confessed his crime with coolness and deliberation. This so enraged the citizens that they took Wallace from the officers, and, dragging him half dead to the scene of his crime, hanged him to the cross beam of a telegraph pole and riddled his limp body with bullets. The news spread from village to village, town to town, throughout the State, and the sentiment of the commonwealth seemed to be that lynch law was the only remedy at hand.

At Minneapolis Chubb McCarthy was in jail awaiting the action of the Grand Jury. His crime had been most flendish, and he had been caught in the very act. There was no question about his guilt, and no circumstances tending to extenuate the crime. At midnight an armed band numbering 200 silently rode into the streets of the town. Guards were posted at the doors of the residences of all the officials, and the streets leading to the jail were thoroughly patrolled. A squad broke the doors of the prison and the jailer was compelled to give up the keys to the culprit's cell. The murderer was taken to the bridge crossing the Soloma River and suspended high in the air over the swollen stream.

At the same hour at Chetopa, another scene was witnessed. John Risbee and Wyley Lee had been arrested by the Marshal and his deputy. In making a desperate attempt to escape they had shot both officers. The Sheriff captured them and held them in the City Hall until the arrival of the train which was to carry them to the county seat. A turbulent crowd gathered about the hall. At 12:30 word was brought that the deputy was dead and the Marshal diving. A special guard had been placed about the building. Suddenly the electric light went out. The officers were speedily overpowered by a quiet but irresistible mob of 300 men. The prisoners were dragged from under a table, where they had crawled in a vain hope of saving their wretched lives. They begged for mercy. For a reply they were dragged into an adjoining room, the windows kicked out, and the doomed men placed on the sill. Ropes were fastened to heavy timbers and around their necks, and against the muzzles of Winchester rifles they were ordered to jump into the street. The strong rope was slack, and as they tumbled from the window they fell a distance of thirty feet, almost to the ground. Bisbee's neck was broken. Lee strangled to death. Then the crowd dispersed. The dead bodies hung from the ropes until 9 o'clock this morning, when they were cut down by the Coroner.

St. Louis, June 27.—A special from Parson, Kan. says: The coroner's jury impaneled at Chetopa yesterday morning to inquire into the lynching of two colored men by a mob of Chetopa citizens Wednesday is composed of four white and eight colored citizens. The white jurors insist that the verdict should say that "the lynched men came to their death by violence at the hands of parties unknown," while the colored jurors say that the names of over one hundred of the mob are known and want the verdict to charge them with the crime, and refuse to consent to a verdict otherwise. Both sides are firm, and it is probable that a majority and minority verdict will be rendered, as the law does not provide for a hung coroner's jury.

Mob Law In Kansas.
It is not often that a coroner's jury is "hung," but that was the condition of one that was impaneled at Chetopa, Kan., on Friday. It was composed of four white and eight colored men, and its duty was to inquire into the lynching of two colored men by a mob of Chetopa citizens. The white jurors wanted to return a verdict that the lynched men came to their death by violence at the hands of unknown parties, and the colored jurors wanted the names of the lynchers stated, because, as it was claimed, they were known.

There is no doubt that the colored jurors were in the right. The lynched men were killed unlawfully, and those who killed them should be made to answer for their deed. The lynched men were guilty of murder. They had attempted to escape from prison, and being discovered shot two of the prison officials, but is there no law in Kansas? Lynch law may be excusable where there is no other law, but there is certainly no necessity for resorting to it in a thickly settled community like that at Chetopa, Kan. There are courts, jails and officials there, and the law ought to be permitted to take its course.

Only a few weeks ago it was discovered that an innocent man had been lynched in New Jersey, and it is quite safe to say that many innocent persons are the victims of lynch law. Four persons have been lynched in Kansas within a week. One lynching leads to another, and if mobs were permitted to deal with those charged with crime, there would soon be a chaotic condition affairs.

The eight colored jurors at Chetopa should remain firm in the stand they have taken, and insist that the names of the lynchers should be made public. If the laws of Kansas are defective let them be amended, but mob law should not be countenanced.

The political caldron is beginning to boil in state politics. More particular in the democratic party, from the fact that it is the dominant party of the state. A furious mob at Chetopa, Kansas, spoiled a couple of republican votes last Thursday by hanging two desperate negroes who had on Monday shot and wounded the city marshal and deputy, while resisting arrest. The negroes were given a few minutes to say their prayers and then swung out the city hall window, hand cuffed together, and were not taken down till about 9 o'clock in the morning. This all took place in the good republican state of Kansas. wyley-lee-chetopa-1888-06-28.A19: THE CHETOPA HANGING.—The Chetopa tragedy, spoken of in these columns last week, was not as serious as first reported, as both officers are alive and there is strong hopes of their recovery. John Risby, one of the negroes, had been drunk, riding horseback down the sidewalks, into stores and wherever he pleased. A warrant was issued for his arrest, and placed in the hands of Marshal Wm. Bentley, who made an unsuccessful attempt to take him, and a man named Ed. Martin was deputized to assist in the arrest. On the appearance of the two officers, Wiley Lee also colored, had joined Risby, and a battle ensued in which the officers were both shot down. The negroes were taken in charge by citizens and held until the arrival of the sheriff. At this point a masked mob broke into the room where the negroes were confined, overpowered the guard, took the prisoners to the rear end of the Statesman printing office and swung them from the second story window where they were found next morning. Risby and Lee came down here on a hand car and stayed several days to avoid being fined for disturbing the peace. After they had started back and gone a short distance the car was wrecked and they walked back and took the train. Among the colored population of this town both men were well known.

Two Colored Men Lynched at Chetopa.

PARSONS, KAN., June 28.—John Kisbee and Wyley Lee, two colored men who were arrested at Chetopa ast evening for shooting City Marshal Wm. Bentley and Deputy Ed. Martin, were lynched this morning at 2 o'clock by a mob of several hundred citizens of Chetopa. The prisoners were in the hands of Sheriff Wilson and a guard, who attempted to take them to the county jail at Oswego, on the north bound Missouri, Kansas & Texas passenger train about midnight last night, but the streets were full of excited and angry people, who notified him that the prisoners must not be taken out of town until a preliminary examination was held. Wilson telegraphed to the county attorney, and returned to the city and placed the prisoners in the city hall. In the meantime the crowd in the streets swelled by the addition of hundreds, who learning the trouble, flocked in from the country, armed with shotguns and whatever weapons they could find. The streets were packed full of people for a distance of three squares on each side of the place where the prisoners were.

At 12:30 o'clock a report was circulated through the crowd that Deputy Marshal Martin had just died from his wounds, and Marshal Bentley was dying. The crowd became wild with rage, and threats of lynching were freely made. Sheriff Wilson doubled the guard over the prisoners, who, struck with terror, begged him to protect them.

About 1 o'clock a mysterious moving was noticed in the crowd and a few moments later the electric light was suddenly extinguished and a moment later somebody in the crowd in front of the city hall shouted: "They are coming." The crowd gave way, and a company of about 200 men filed through it and up the stairs into the city hall. Sheriff Wilson fought desperately to protect his prisoners and severely wounded one of the mob in the face by a blow from his revolver. He and his men were soon overpowered and the mob had possession.

On December 24 last, a book agent named H. H. Pelton was canvassing in Fort Scott for subscribers to a work sold only on subscription. There is a city ordinance requiring "drummers" to pay a license fee, which for book and map agents is $1 a day or $55 a year. Pelton did not procure a license, and a complaint was filed against him in the police court. He was arrested, found guilty and fined. He appealed to the district court and was again defeated and assessed $25 and costs, when he finally carried his case to the supreme court. The main question involved was, whether a city "may be empowered by the laws of its own state to impose a license tax upon a commercial 'drummer' or other person of another state for merely offering to sell goods within the city by sample." The court holds that this question has been settled by the supreme court of the United States in favor of the "drummer," and reverses the decision of the court below. A whole page of authorities are cited.
